entries.reason: Empty carets now agree as Superscript([]). The remaining difference is double-tilde ownership: an unmatched ~~ is Text under the shared strikethrough rule, while this Pandoc reader emits Subscript([]).
Markdown Core retains inherited declarations before occurrence declarations, preserving every duplicate; Pandoc combineAttr instead deduplicates and reprioritizes declarations.

A class= value splits where HTML splits a class attribute: tab, LF, FF, CR and space. NBSP, IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE and a vertical tab from a character reference stay inside the class; Pandoc splits at every Unicode space.
Markdown Core has no numbered examples: `(@label)` is ordinary text and a bare `@label` is a bibliography citation. Pandoc emits example List items and replaces references with derived numbering.

This compound reader omits all_symbols_escapable, so successful script escapes also differ because of oracle configuration. An isolated control with that prerequisite agrees. The real contextual difference is that only committed product scripts decode escaped ASCII space to NBSP; outside or failed scripts retain inherited literal spelling.
Character-reference whitespace is decoded content and never a raw-whitespace boundary for script matching. Markdown Core preserves a decoded TAB; Pandoc normalizes it to an ASCII space.

Empty carets now form Superscript nodes. Core retains each authored adjacent pair and its scope (^^^^ gives two empty nodes); Pandoc combines adjacent Superscript values. The remaining tilde differences follow maximal-run ownership: two tildes are strikethrough, longer runs are text.
Complete code tokens own their bytes, including whitespace and script delimiter characters, before the delimiter engine sees them.
Markdown Core reserves every explicit declaration across the whole document before generating anchors; Pandoc allocates this heading before it sees the later explicit heading identifier.
Markdown Core filters every scalar uniformly and has no emoji alias step; Pandoc converts the grinning-face scalar to its grinning alias during GFM anchor generation.
Markdown Core applies Unicode 17 simple lowercase (U+0130 becomes U+0069); Pandoc expands U+0130 to U+0069 U+0307 with full lowercase.
Markdown Core maps each Unicode White_Space scalar to a hyphen, including U+0085 and U+2028; Pandoc removes those two scalars from this heading anchor.
Markdown Core reserves identifiers on every emitted kind before heading synthesis; Pandoc does not reserve the code identifier against its heading registry.

Markdown Core has no implicit heading references: a heading declares no reference label, so `[Heading]` stays bracket text unless a link reference definition declares the label. Pandoc's implicit_header_references resolves it to the heading.
The shared anchor registry reserves explicit Span identifiers across the whole document before heading synthesis. Pandoc generates the earlier heading before reading the later Span identifier.
Both affixes exclude raw leading and trailing whitespace under the citation module. Pandoc retains a leading suffix space before nested brackets; nested owners and their content remain compared.

The tail key now belongs to the outer Cite as a normal item, agreeing with Pandoc. Only the declared affix trimming remains different: Core stores [p. 7] while Pandoc retains the leading space before that suffix.
Generated anchors concatenate the stored, trimmed citation prefix, @key and suffix per item. Pandoc uses the authored fallback spelling with separator spaces; its suffix also retains a leading space.
The key opener precondition forbids a preceding underscore as well as Unicode letters and numbers. Pandoc accepts a citation after underscore.

Under CommonMark only a list starting at 1 may interrupt a paragraph, so the indented `2. ordinary` stays a lazy continuation of the parent paragraph in Core. Pandoc puts the line in another Plain block. The following `1. nested` starts a nested list on both sides.

A non-resolving reference tail does not block a complete bibliography group. Pandoc leaves the first brackets literal and parses their key as authorInText.

The inherited reference-definition grammar registers the authored @a label, but a complete citation group wins over its shortcut. Pandoc parses the declaration-shaped line as a citation followed by text.

A braced key excludes whitespace, which is a space, a tab or a line ending (docs/specs/dialect.md), so NBSP and IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE are key characters. Pandoc's reader excludes every Unicode space and keeps both candidates as text. Both reject the ASCII space.
The dialect keeps only decimal list markers, so `h. eight` and `i. nine` are one paragraph in Core. This control reader omits Pandoc's startnum and makes a lower-alpha list starting at 1.
Markdown Core has no nameless fenced divs: every container is named, `:::name`, so `::: {.class}` and `::: class` lines are paragraph text. Pandoc's fenced_divs reads them as Divs.

The product retains the authored term-gap compact flag even when the first body contains no top-level paragraph (nested definition list, code or an empty body). Pandoc stores tightness through Plain/Para and has no corresponding flag in these shapes; its projection records null rather than inventing one. All terms and ordered bodies remain compared.

A bare attribute is valid in the dialect's own grammar and is recorded as `disabled="true"`, so `[text]{disabled}` is a Span; Pandoc's bracketed_spans reader rejects a member with no `=` and keeps the bytes as text.

A class name is taken as written, so `[x]{.1}` is a Span with class `1`; Pandoc requires a class to begin with a letter and keeps the bytes as text. The three malformed containers that follow agree as text, and the closing `[y]{.d}` agrees as a Span.
Only `:` marks a definition body: the dialect dropped Pandoc's `~` marker, so Core reads each `~` line as paragraph text, while Pandoc's definition_lists reader makes a DefinitionList.

Only `:` marks a definition body: the dialect dropped Pandoc's `~` marker, so Core reads each `~` line as paragraph text, while Pandoc's definition_lists reader makes a DefinitionList. Here the lone `~` and the indented `body` are one paragraph's lines in Core.
The dialect dropped Pandoc's `{-}` shorthand: a lone `-` is a name like any other, so Core reads `{-}` as the bare record `-="true"`, while Pandoc reads it as the class `unnumbered`.

The dialect keeps only decimal list markers with `.` or `)`: Pandoc's fancy_lists letters, Roman numerals, `#` and both-sided parentheses are text in Core, while Pandoc makes ordered lists of them. Here the decimal `9)` list agrees and the Roman sublist is a paragraph in Core.
